subsystems.name: Growing structure
subsystems.role: stacks plants in layers to multiply the growing area per square metre of floor.

subsystems.name: Lighting
subsystems.role: replaces sunlight with tuned spectra, usually pink or magenta blends of red and blue.

subsystems.name: Root-zone delivery
subsystems.role: feeds water and nutrients directly to the roots.

subsystems.name: Climate control
subsystems.role: holds temperature, humidity, CO₂ and airflow in the narrow band crops tolerate.

subsystems.name: Sensing and control
subsystems.role: keeps every tray on the same recipe and flags problems early.

subsystems.name: Facade and building interface
subsystems.role: where the idea meets architecture: glazing, insulation and heat exchange between the farm and the occupied floors.

buildSteps.title: Choose the site
buildSteps.detail: A building with high floors, strong floor loadings, spare electrical capacity and cheap low-carbon power suits this better than a light industrial shed.

buildSteps.title: Design the layers
buildSteps.detail: Rack heights and aisle widths are set so plants get even light and workers or robots can reach every tray.

buildSteps.title: Install the structure
buildSteps.detail: Galvanised steel racks are bolted in and levelled; drainage and cable routes run underneath.

buildSteps.title: Fit lighting
buildSteps.detail: LED bars are mounted above each tier and tuned per crop — more red for leaf growth, more blue to shape plant form.

buildSteps.title: Plumb the nutrient loop
buildSteps.detail: Pumps, tanks and dosing units are connected into a closed loop; water is filtered and sterilised so it can be recirculated for weeks rather than dumped.

buildSteps.title: Close the climate
buildSteps.detail: The room is sealed and insulated, then heat pumps, dehumidifiers and fans are commissioned to hold the set points.

buildSteps.title: Automate seeding and harvest
buildSteps.detail: Seed is sown into trays or plugs, moved by conveyor or robot, and cut and packed on site.

buildSteps.title: Integrate with the building
buildSteps.detail: Waste heat from the LEDs is recovered for hot water or space heating; the facade is detailed for daylight, shading and fire safety.

prerequisites.why: lighting is the single largest electricity cost, so efficiency decides whether a crop is viable.
soil-free root zones cut water use and allow tight control of nutrients.

prerequisites.tech: Sealed climate control with heat pumps
prerequisites.why: consistent conditions are what make yields predictable indoors.
without it, indoor staples cannot compete with field-grown grain on cost.
labour is the second biggest cost after energy; handling trays by machine changes the economics.

prerequisites.tech: Crop varieties bred for indoor life
prerequisites.why: short, high-density, low-light varieties are still mostly selected rather than purpose-bred.

pathway.milestone: warehouse-scale vertical farms supplying leafy greens and herbs to nearby supermarkets
pathway.unlocks: year-round local salad with very low water use and no pesticide residue.

pathway.milestone: larger, more automated farms and a wider crop list such as berries and soft fruit
pathway.unlocks: better use of capital and a bigger share of the fresh-produce market.

pathway.milestone: farms genuinely built into building skins and rooftops, sharing heat and power with occupants
pathway.unlocks: food grown where it is eaten, with waste heat doing double duty.

pathway.milestone: staple crops such as wheat and rice grown economically indoors
pathway.unlocks: meaningful substitution for field agriculture — only if energy becomes very cheap and clean.
